reference.source: Clinical neuromuscular and medical genetics references
clinicalPearls: POMT1 encodes protein O-mannosyltransferase 1, which initiates O-mannosyl glycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan; loss of function disrupts the glycan that bridges muscle and brain basement membranes to the extracellular matrix.

It is the archetypal cause of Walker-Warburg syndrome, the most severe end of the dystroglycanopathy spectrum, presenting at birth with profound hypotonia, weakness and a raised serum creatine kinase.
The classic triad combines congenital muscular dystrophy, a cobblestone (type II) lissencephaly with neuronal overmigration, and structural eye malformations.
Brain imaging typically shows cobblestone cortex, hydrocephalus, a kinked or hypoplastic brainstem, cerebellar hypoplasia with cysts and absent or thin corpus callosum.
Milder allelic phenotypes exist, spanning muscle-eye-brain-like disease and limb-girdle muscular dystrophy with or without intellectual disability, depending on residual enzyme activity.
Ocular findings may include microphthalmia, cataract, retinal dysplasia or detachment, buphthalmos and optic nerve hypoplasia.
Immunohistochemistry of muscle shows reduced or absent glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan despite preserved core protein, the hallmark of a dystroglycanopathy.
Inheritance is autosomal recessive, so both parents are typically unaffected carriers and recurrence risk is substantial for future pregnancies.
reference.pathophysiology: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in POMT1 abolish or reduce protein O-mannosyltransferase 1 activity. Working in an obligate complex with POMT2, this enzyme catalyses the first committed step of O-mannosylation, attaching mannose to serine and threonine residues of alpha-dystroglycan. This initiates assembly of the matriglycan chain that allows alpha-dystroglycan to bind laminin, agrin, perlecan and neurexin in the basement membrane. When glycosylation fails, alpha-dystroglycan can no longer anchor the sarcolemma or the pial glia-limitans to the extracellular matrix. In muscle this produces membrane fragility and a dystrophic process; in brain the breached glia-limitans permits neurones to overmigrate beyond the cortical surface, generating cobblestone lissencephaly; and in the developing eye disrupted matrix interactions cause the characteristic malformations. The severity of the phenotype correlates broadly with the amount of residual functional glycosyltransferase activity.
additionalDifferentials: Other congenital muscular dystrophies with structural brain involvement
Congenital myotonic dystrophy and congenital myopathies with hypotonia
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI to characterise cobblestone cortex, brainstem and cerebellar anomalies and hydrocephalus
Ophthalmological assessment including examination for microphthalmia, cataract and retinal dysplasia
Muscle biopsy with immunohistochemistry for glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan
Molecular genetic testing of POMT1 and a dystroglycanopathy gene panel
Electromyography and nerve conduction studies where diagnosis is uncertain
Prenatal or fetal imaging and genetic counselling for at-risk pregnancies
redFlags: Progressive hydrocephalus with raised intracranial pressure requiring urgent neurosurgical assessment
Neonatal respiratory failure or feeding failure with aspiration risk
Seizures, particularly in the neonatal period
Rapidly worsening vision or signs of retinal detachment
Recurrent chest infections from respiratory muscle weakness
reference.prognosis: The Walker-Warburg end of the POMT1 spectrum carries a very poor prognosis, with most severely affected infants dying within the first years of life. Milder allelic forms, including limb-girdle presentations, can be compatible with prolonged survival, though with variable weakness and cognitive involvement.
pitfalls: Assuming a normal-appearing muscle biopsy core protein excludes dystroglycanopathy; the defect is in glycosylation, not the protein itself.
Attributing the brain malformation to an acquired antenatal insult rather than a genetic glycosylation defect.
Overlooking subtle ocular malformations that help distinguish dystroglycanopathies from other congenital muscular dystrophies.
Failing to recognise milder limb-girdle phenotypes as allelic to the severe congenital form.
Not offering genetic counselling and recurrence-risk discussion once autosomal recessive inheritance is confirmed.
references: Standard textbooks of paediatric neurology and neuromuscular disease
management: Supportive, multidisciplinary care as no disease-specific or curative therapy exists for the dystroglycanopathy
Ventriculoperitoneal shunting for hydrocephalus and antiseizure medication for epilepsy
Respiratory support and gastrostomy feeding for weakness, bulbar dysfunction and recurrent aspiration
Ophthalmological management of structural eye malformations such as cataract, retinal detachment and glaucoma
Physiotherapy, occupational therapy and orthopaedic management of contractures, with seating and postural support
Palliative and family-centred care planning for the severe Walker-Warburg end of the spectrum given its very poor prognosis
Genetic counselling, carrier testing and prenatal or preimplantation diagnosis given autosomal recessive POMT1 inheritance
